subject: Pathology
summary: Constrictive pericarditis is fibrotic thickening of the pericardium that limits ventricular filling, causing right‑sided heart failure signs. Diagnosis relies on imaging, hemodynamics and exclusion of restrictive cardiomyopathy.

sections.p: A rigid, often calcified pericardium encases the heart, preventing normal diastolic expansion. Diagnosis requires at least two of: pericardial thickening >4 mm on CT/MRI, septal bounce on echo, equalization of diastolic pressures, and clinical signs of right‑sided congestion.
b: Imaging shows thickened, sometimes calcified pericardium.
Hemodynamics reveal dip‑and‑plateau waveform and equal diastolic pressures.

sections.p: Severity is staged by symptom burden and hemodynamic compromise: mild (asymptomatic, normal exercise tolerance), moderate (exertional dyspnoea, peripheral oedema), severe (resting dyspnoea, hepatic congestion, low cardiac output).
b: Mild: no functional limitation.
Moderate: NYHA II‑III, mild hepatic congestion.
Severe: NYHA IV, hypotension, organ hypoperfusion.

sections.p: Infectious and inflammatory processes dominate worldwide, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Tuberculosis (most common globally).
Post‑viral or bacterial pericarditis.
Cardiac surgery or pericardiotomy.
Radiation therapy (especially for thoracic malignancies).
Asbestos exposure, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin.

sections.p: Patients develop right‑sided heart failure signs with preserved left‑sided function.
b: Peripheral oedema, ascites, hepatomegaly.
Elevated JVP with Kussmaul sign (rise on inspiration).
Pericardial knock early in diastole.
Low‑voltage ECG, possible calcification on chest X‑ray.

sections.p: Combine bedside, imaging and invasive studies to confirm constriction and exclude mimics.

t.b: Does the heart show septal bounce and respiratory variation in mitral inflow? → Positive findings support constriction; if unavailable, proceed to CT/MRI.
Is the pericardium >4 mm thick or calcified? → Confirms anatomic restriction; MRI also assesses inflammation.
Are diastolic pressures equalized with a dip‑and‑plateau waveform? → Hemodynamic confirmation; essential when echo/CT are equivocal.
Is there pericardial calcification? → Suggestive but not definitive; useful where advanced imaging is unavailable.
Is TB infection present? → Guides antimicrobial therapy; if unavailable, treat empirically in high‑prevalence areas.

sections.p: Unchecked constriction leads to irreversible organ damage.
b: Progressive hepatic failure (jaundice, coagulopathy).
Renal dysfunction from low output.
Cardiogenic shock after minor stress.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve inflammation, and restore cardiac filling by pericardiectomy when indicated.
b: Anti‑TB therapy for confirmed or probable tuberculosis.
NSAIDs or colchicine for inflammatory pericarditis when infection excluded.
Pericardiectomy (complete removal of fibrous pericardium) for symptomatic severe disease.
Diuretics for volume overload; avoid over‑diuresis that reduces preload excessively.

sections.p: Monitor for recurrence, residual heart failure and complications of surgery.
b: Serial echo at 3‑month intervals for the first year.
Assess functional status (NYHA class) and liver/kidney labs.
Vaccinate against TB and maintain infection control in endemic regions.

sections.p: Conditions that also limit ventricular filling but have different pathology.
b: Restrictive cardiomyopathy – myocardial infiltration, normal pericardium.
Right‑sided heart failure from pulmonary hypertension.
Cardiac tamponade – fluid, not fibrous shell.

sections.p: Certain findings may appear normal despite severe disease.
b: Normal pericardial thickness on echo if imaging window is poor; CT/MRI needed.
Low‑voltage ECG may be absent in early disease.
JVP may be normal at rest; look for Kussmaul sign during inspiration.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of dyspnoea with hypotension
Rapidly increasing abdominal distension and jaundice

faq.q: Why does constriction cause a pericardial knock?
faq.a: The rigid pericardium abruptly halts early diastolic filling, producing a high‑pitched early diastolic sound.

faq.q: Can constrictive pericarditis resolve without surgery?
faq.a: Rarely; only if the cause is an active infection or inflammation treated early. Most fibrotic cases need pericardiectomy.
A rise in JVP on inspiration indicates impaired right‑ventricular filling, a hallmark of constriction.

exam: Explain how you would differentiate constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy using imaging and haemodynamics.
List the three most common causes of constrictive pericarditis worldwide and the first‑line treatment for each.
Describe the pathophysiological basis of the pericardial knock and Kussmaul sign.
